key: SS.HIST.L04.02|Is an encyclopedia page about Baltimore primary, or secondary? Secondary, or primary?

SS.HIST.L04.02|Your friend tells a story he heard from you. Is that first-hand, or second-hand? Second-hand, or first-hand?
how: If you saw a ballgame, your story is first-hand, primary. If your friend tells it after hearing from you, it is second-hand, secondary.

key: SS.HIST.L04.02|Is a photo taken at the event primary? Yes, or no?
how: Just one kind: a photo taken at the time is primary.

key: SS.HIST.L04.02|An old oil lamp is from long ago, or today? Long ago, or today?
how: Skill underneath: Long Ago and Today (Level 1). Things from long ago tell us how people lived.

how: Maps have a grid of lines to find any place. Latitude lines go across, east to west. They tell how far north or south a place is from the equator.

key: SS.HIST.L05.01|In what year did Columbus sail? 1492, 1776, or 1620?
how: In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west from Spain with three ships. He wanted to reach Asia. Instead he reached islands near America that Europeans did not know about.
pic: ⛵ Niña  ⛵ Pinta  ⛵ Santa María — 1492

key: SS.HIST.L05.01|What happened to the Jews of Spain in 1492? They were forced to leave Spain, they sailed with Columbus to Asia, or they became the rulers of Spain?
how: 1492 was also a sad year for the Jews. That same year, Spain forced all Jews to leave. Many went to Portugal, North Africa and the Ottoman Empire (Turkey).

key: SS.HIST.L05.01|Whose ships first sailed all the way around the world? Magellan's, Columbus's, or Lincoln's?
how: Explorers sailed to map the world. Ferdinand Magellan's ships were the first to sail all the way around the world, from 1519 to 1522.

key: SS.HIST.L05.01|Did Columbus sail in 1492? Yes, or no?

how: Skill underneath: Timelines (Level 3). Earlier years come first.

key: SS.HIST.L05.02|How many colonies did England start on America's east coast? 13, 50, or 5?
how: A colony is land ruled by a country far away. England started 13 colonies along America's Atlantic coast. Later they became the first 13 states.

key: SS.HIST.L05.02|Our city, Baltimore, is named after whom? Lord Baltimore, Christopher Columbus, or Rabbi Rice?
how: Jamestown, Virginia (1607) was the first English colony town that lasted. Maryland was started in 1634 by Lord Baltimore's family. Our city is named for him!

key: SS.HIST.L05.02|What were the northern colonies called? New England, the Midwest, or the Southwest?
how: The colonies are in three groups: New England in the north, the Middle colonies, and the Southern colonies. Maryland was a Southern colony.

SS.HIST.L05.02|Who was in charge of the branch? England, or the colonies themselves?
how: Think of a branch office of a big company in another city. A colony was like England's branch across the ocean.

key: SS.HIST.L05.02|Were there 13 colonies? Yes, or no?
how: Just one number: there were 13 colonies.

key: SS.HIST.L05.02|Were the colonies on the east coast, or the west coast? The east coast, or the west coast?
how: Skill underneath: Regions of the United States (Level 5). The 13 colonies were in today's Northeast and Southeast.

key: SS.JHIST.L05.01|How many Jews arrived in New Amsterdam in 1654? 23, 1,000, or 2?
how: In 1654, 23 Jews arrived in New Amsterdam (today New York). They came from Recife, Brazil, running from the Portuguese, who did not let Jews live there freely.

key: SS.JHIST.L05.01|Who fought for the Jews' right to stand guard like everyone else? Asser Levy, Peter Stuyvesant, or Columbus?
how: The governor, Peter Stuyvesant, did not want them. But the company that owned the colony let them stay. Asser Levy fought for the right to stand guard and own property like everyone else.

how: Imagine moving to a new school where some boys say you can't play. You ask the rebbe kindly, and he says you can. That's like what happened in New Amsterdam.

key: SS.JHIST.L05.01|Did Jews come to New Amsterdam in 1654? Yes, or no?
how: Just one fact: the first Jews came to New Amsterdam in 1654.

key: SS.JHIST.L05.01|In 1492, Jews were forced out of which country? Spain, or America?
how: Skill underneath: Explorers and 1492 (Level 5). In 1492 Jews were forced out of Spain, and many wandered to new lands.

key: SS.HIST.L05.03|Did the Pilgrims come on the Mayflower? Yes, or no?
how: Just one fact: the Pilgrims came on the Mayflower.

key: SS.HIST.L05.03|What is Thanksgiving about? Giving thanks, or getting presents?
how: Skill underneath: Our Country: America (Level 1). Thanksgiving is an American holiday for giving thanks.

key: SS.HIST.L06.01|What did colonists throw into Boston Harbor in 1773? Tea, gold, or newspapers?
how: In 1773, colonists in Boston threw a load of taxed British tea into the harbor. This was the Boston Tea Party. In 1775, fighting began, and the American Revolution started.

key: SS.HIST.L06.01|The Stamp Act taxed what? Paper, like newspapers, water, or horses?
pic: 1765 Stamp Act → 1773 Boston Tea Party → 1775 fighting begins → 1776 Declaration → 1783 war ends

pic: 1765 Stamp Act → 1773 Boston Tea Party → 1775 fighting begins → 1776 Declaration → 1783 war ends

pic: 1765 Stamp Act → 1773 Boston Tea Party → 1775 fighting begins → 1776 Declaration → 1783 war ends

how: Just one: a tax is money people must pay the government.

key: SS.HIST.L06.02|On what date was the Declaration of Independence signed? July 4, 1776, July 4, 1492, or November 1863?
how: On July 4, 1776, leaders of the colonies signed the Declaration of Independence. It said the colonies were now free from Britain. That is why July 4 is America's birthday.

how: Just one fact: the Declaration was signed on July 4, 1776.

key: SS.JHIST.L06.01|Who was the first Jew to die for American independence? Francis Salvador, Haym Salomon, or Asser Levy?
how: Francis Salvador of South Carolina was the first Jew elected to a colonial government. In 1776 he was killed in battle, the first Jew to die for American independence.

key: SS.CIV.L06.01|What is it called when each branch can stop the others from going too far? Checks and balances, taxes, or a timeline?
how: Each branch can check the others. The President can veto (say no to) a law. Congress can still pass it with enough votes. This is called checks and balances.

SS.CIV.L06.02|Who wrote 'to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance'? George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, or Haym Salomon?
SS.CIV.L06.02|Can the government tell you how to daven? No, or yes?
how: Just one freedom: freedom of religion means the government may not tell you how to worship.

key: SS.CIV.L06.02|The Bill of Rights was added to which document? The Constitution, or a song?
how: Skill underneath: The Constitution and Three Branches (Level 6). The Constitution is the plan for America's government.

key: SS.JHIST.L06.02|In which city did Rebecca Gratz live? Philadelphia, Baltimore, or Newport?
how: Rebecca Gratz lived in Philadelphia (1781-1869). She spent her life helping others: orphans, poor families and Jewish children who needed to learn.

key: SS.JHIST.L06.02|What did Rebecca Gratz start in 1838? The first Jewish Sunday school in America, the B&O Railroad, or the Constitution?
how: In 1838, Rebecca Gratz started the Hebrew Sunday School, the first Jewish Sunday school in America. Jewish children could learn about their religion there.

key: SS.JHIST.L06.02|Which Jewish value was the center of her life? Chessed, kindness to others, getting rich, or being famous?
how: She also helped start a home for orphans in 1815 and a Jewish foster home in 1855. Chessed, kindness to others, was the center of her life.

SS.JHIST.L06.02|Rebecca Gratz helped orphans, poor families and children. What do we call that kindness? Chessed, taxes, or exploring?
SS.JHIST.L06.02|What did Rebecca Gratz do for others? Helped them, or ignored them?
how: Think of a candle that lights other candles without losing its own light. Rebecca Gratz helped many others, and her good name still shines.

key: SS.JHIST.L06.02|Did Rebecca Gratz live in Philadelphia? Yes, or no?
how: Just one fact: Rebecca Gratz lived in Philadelphia.

key: SS.HIST.L07.02|Which empire destroyed the first Beis Hamikdash? Bavel, Rome, or Greece?
how: Bavel (Babylon) was a powerful empire between two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, in today's Iraq. Its king, Nevuchadnetzar, destroyed the first Beis Hamikdash and took the Jews into exile in Bavel.

key: SS.HIST.L07.02|What does exile (galus) mean? Being forced to live away from your land, a big holiday, or a kind of river?
how: Exile (galus) means being forced to live away from your land. In Bavel, Jews kept the Torah, davened and learned. Bavel later became a great center of Torah learning.

how: Before the Churban, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked the Roman general for Yavneh and its sages. In Yavneh, Torah learning continued after the Beis Hamikdash was gone.

key: SS.JHIST.L08.01|What were the heads of the yeshivos in Bavel called after the Gemara? The Geonim, the Amoraim, or the Chashmonaim?
how: After the Gemara was completed, the heads of the great yeshivos in Bavel were called the Geonim. Jews all over the world sent them questions, and they answered with letters called teshuvos.

key: SS.JHIST.L08.01|In which country did Rashi live? France, Egypt, or Bavel?
how: Rashi was born in France in 1040. He wrote a clear commentary on Chumash and on most of the Gemara. Boys all over the world still learn with Rashi every day.
pic: GEONIM (Bavel, after the Gemara) → RISHONIM (about 1000-1500)\n📖 Rashi: France, born 1040\n📖 Rambam: born in Spain 1138, lived in Egypt

key: SS.JHIST.L08.01|Which great sefer did the Rambam write? The Mishneh Torah, the Talmud Bavli, or the Declaration of Independence?
how: The Rambam was born in Spain in 1138. His family had to flee, and he settled in Egypt, where he was a doctor to the ruler. He wrote the Mishneh Torah, a code of all of halacha.

key: SS.HIST.L08.01|In what year did the First Crusade attack the Jews of the Rhineland? 1096, 1492, or 1914?
how: In 1096, armies called Crusaders marched from Europe toward Eretz Yisroel. On the way, they attacked and killed many Jews in the Rhineland towns of Speyer, Worms and Mainz.

key: SS.JHIST.L08.02|What is an expulsion? Forcing a group to leave a country, a kind of holiday, or a new law about taxes?
how: An expulsion is when a ruler forces a group of people to leave the country. In the Middle Ages, many countries expelled their Jews.

key: SS.JHIST.L08.02|Which country expelled its Jews first? England, Spain, or Portugal?
how: England expelled its Jews in 1290. France expelled its Jews in 1306. Spain in 1492, and Portugal in 1497.

key: SS.JHIST.L08.02|How did Doña Gracia Nasi help Jews? She helped them escape to safe lands, she was a Crusader, or she wrote the Mishneh Torah?
how: Doña Gracia Nasi was a rich Jewish woman from Portugal. She used her money to help thousands of Jews escape to safe lands, like the Ottoman Empire.

key: SS.JHIST.L08.03|What was the Council of Four Lands? A council of rabbanim and leaders who ran Jewish community life, a Polish army, or a kind of castle?
how: For hundreds of years, Poland and Lithuania had huge Jewish communities. The Council of Four Lands (Vaad Arba Aratzos) was a council of rabbanim and leaders who ran Jewish community life.

key: SS.JHIST.L08.03|Who began the Chassidic movement? The Baal Shem Tov, the Vilna Gaon, or Rashi?
how: The Baal Shem Tov (1698-1760) began the Chassidic movement. The Vilna Gaon (1720-1797), in Vilna, Lithuania, was one of the greatest Torah scholars ever.

key: SS.JHIST.L08.03|What did Sarah Schenirer start in 1917? The first Bais Yaakov school, the first railroad, or the first yeshiva in Bavel?
how: In 1917, Sarah Schenirer started the first Bais Yaakov school, in Krakow, Poland, so Jewish girls could learn Torah. Today there are Bais Yaakov schools around the world.

how: From 1880 to 1924, about two million Jews came to America from Eastern Europe. They escaped poverty and pogroms, violent attacks on Jewish towns.

key: SS.JHIST.L08.04|Who led the Nazi party? Adolf Hitler, Abraham Lincoln, or Alexander the Great?
how: In 1933, the Nazi party, led by Adolf Hitler, took power in Germany. The Nazis hated Jews. Soon they made laws that took away Jews' rights.
pic: 1933 Nazis take power → 1935 laws take away Jews' rights → 1938 Kristallnacht → 1939 war begins → 1945 war ends

key: SS.JHIST.L08.04|What happened on Kristallnacht? Nazis burned shuls and attacked Jewish stores, a war ended, or a new school opened?
how: On Kristallnacht, November 9-10, 1938, Nazis burned hundreds of shuls and broke the windows of Jewish stores across Germany and Austria.
pic: 1933 Nazis take power → 1935 laws take away Jews' rights → 1938 Kristallnacht → 1939 war begins → 1945 war ends

key: SS.CIV.L09.02|What does 'dina d'malchusa dina' mean? The law of the land is the law, the king is always right, or there are no laws?
how: The Gemara teaches 'dina d'malchusa dina': the law of the land is the law. Jews must keep the fair laws of the country they live in, like paying taxes honestly.

key: SS.HIST.L09.02|Why was it called the 'Cold' War? The two sides never fought each other directly, it was fought only in winter, or it was fought in Antarctica?
how: After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union became rivals. This long struggle, from about 1947 to 1991, is called the Cold War, because the two never fought each other directly.

key: SS.HIST.L09.02|What was a refusenik? A Soviet Jew who was refused permission to leave, a kind of soldier, or a Soviet leader?
how: The Soviet government did not allow Jews to learn Torah or teach Hebrew freely. Jews who asked to leave and were refused were called refuseniks. Some, like Natan Sharansky, were put in prison.

key: SS.HIST.L09.02|In what year did the Soviet Union end? 1991, 1945, or 1776?
how: In 1987, about 250,000 people rallied in Washington, D.C. for Soviet Jews. The Berlin Wall fell in 1989, and the Soviet Union ended in 1991. About one million Soviet Jews moved to Israel, and many came to America.

key: SS.GEO.L10.01|What is climate? The usual weather of a place over many years, the weather today only, or a kind of map key?
how: Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. The earth has four main climate zones: tropical, dry, temperate and polar. Distance from the equator is one big reason they differ.
pic:
CLIMATE ZONES
🌴 Tropical: near the equator, hot and rainy
🏜️ Dry: deserts, very little rain
🍂 Temperate: four seasons (like Baltimore)
🧊 Polar: near the poles, very cold

key: SS.GEO.L10.01|Which climate zone is Baltimore in? Temperate, tropical, or polar?
how: Tropical places, near the equator, are hot and rainy, like rainforests. Polar places, near the North and South Poles, are very cold. Temperate places, like Baltimore, have four seasons.

key: SS.GEO.L10.01|What does population density measure? How many people live in each square mile, how hot a place is, or how much it rains?
how: People most often live where there is fresh water, good farmland and a mild climate. Population density means how many people live in each square mile.

key: SS.HIST.L10.02|What was one big effect of the printing press? Books became cheaper and more people could read, books disappeared, or only kings could read?
how: Printed books were faster and cheaper to make. More people could own books and learn to read, and new ideas spread quickly.

key: SS.HIST.L10.02|Where was the whole Talmud Bavli first printed (1520-1523)? Venice, Baltimore, or Athens?
how: Jews were early printers. Hebrew seforim were printed in Italy in the 1470s. From 1520 to 1523, Daniel Bomberg printed the whole Talmud Bavli in Venice, and its page layout is still used today.

key: SS.JHIST.L10.01|Which empire welcomed many Jews after 1492? The Ottoman Empire, the Roman Empire, or the British Empire?
how: After Spain expelled its Jews in 1492, the Ottoman Empire (Turkey) welcomed many of them. Jewish communities grew in Istanbul, Salonika and Eretz Yisroel, which the Ottomans ruled.

key: SS.JHIST.L10.01|Who added notes to the Shulchan Aruch for Ashkenazim? The Rama, Rav Yosef Karo, or Gutenberg?
how: Rav Moshe Isserles (the Rama) in Krakow added notes for Ashkenazim, called the Mapa. The Arizal also taught Torah in Tzfas in those years.

key: SS.CIV.L10.01|What does a government do? Makes and enforces a country's rules, grows all the food, or writes all the books?

key: SS.CIV.L10.01|In which kind of government does one ruler hold all power with no free elections? A dictatorship, a democracy, or a republic?
how: In a monarchy, a king or queen rules, often passing power down in the family. In a dictatorship, one ruler holds all power, with no free elections and no free speech.
